Compare models' predictive scores, with standard errors that respect the data

Source: R/ilm_compare.R, R/zzz-iml-aliases.R
ilm_compare.Rd

Compares the scores of two or more models on the same rows: the mean difference in a score, its standard error, and a test of whether it is zero. The first model is the reference. Every other model is compared with it, as that model's mean score minus the reference's. Scores are losses, so a negative difference means the model predicts better than the reference.

Usage

ilm_compare(..., rule = NULL, by = "row", lag = NULL, method = NULL)

Arguments

...

Two or more tables of scores for the same rows, in the same order, such as the output of the scoring of an "ilm_pred". Name them (ilm_compare(ar = s1, iid = s2)) to label the comparison.

rule

The score to compare: the name of a score column. By default the first score in the table, which for a plain data frame is its first column named after a rule (log, crps, brier, pinball_*, interval_*, wis, squared, absolute, mase or rmsse).

by

"row", "origin", or the name of a column the rows are clustered by, such as "group" or "fold". See Why the standard error depends on by.

lag

Only for by = "origin" with method = "dm": the truncation lag of the long-run variance, that is, how many autocovariances of the per-origin mean differences it keeps.

  • The default suits origins one time step apart. Forecasts h steps ahead from neighbouring origins then overlap in h - 1 steps, so the pooled row uses the longest horizon minus one, and horizon h's own row uses h - 1.

  • Set it yourself when the origins are further apart. With origins s time steps apart, forecasts h ahead overlap in ceiling(h / s) - 1 of them, so use lag = ceiling(H / s) - 1 for a longest horizon H. It is 0 when the origins are at least H apart, and the forecasts do not overlap.

  • A value you give applies to the pooled row and to every horizon's row. It must be between 0 and the number of origins minus 1.

  • If the variance it gives is negative, it is taken as 0 and the null hypothesis rejected (statistic infinite, p-value 0), as Diebold and Mariano (1995, section 1.1) prescribe, and the test warns.

With method = "wpe", or any by other than "origin", giving lag is an error. The fixed-smoothing test chooses its own bandwidth from the number of origins, whatever their spacing.

method

Only for by = "origin": which Diebold-Mariano test.

  • "wpe", the default: the fixed-smoothing test of Coroneo and Iacone (2020, section 4.2). The variance of the T per-origin mean differences is their periodogram averaged over the first m = floor(T^(1/3)) Fourier frequencies (equation (8); the bandwidth of their simulations, section 5). The statistic is referred to t on 2m degrees of freedom (equation (9)). It needs at least 3 origins and takes no lag. In limn's simulation it held its size from 10 origins up.

  • "dm": the usual test. It uses a long-run variance truncated at lag with equal weights (Diebold and Mariano 1995, section 1.1), Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold's (1997) correction (equation (9), p. 283), and t on T - 1 degrees of freedom (pp. 283-284). Use it to compare with published results. With fewer than about 100 origins over several horizons it rejects too often, and warns.

Giving method with any by other than "origin" is an error. See Why the standard error depends on by.

Value

A data frame of class "ilm_compare", one row per comparison, with the two mean scores, their difference, its standard error, the test statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value, the number of rows and of clusters, and the method. For by = "origin" with several horizons, each comparison has a row pooled over the horizons (horizon is NA) and a row for each horizon.

The test is also given as data, so nothing needs reading from method, which describes it in words:

  • test: "independent" (by = "row"), "clustered", "wpe" or "dm" (by = "origin").

  • bandwidth: for "wpe", the number m of Fourier frequencies averaged; otherwise NA.

  • lag: for "dm", the truncation lag used; otherwise NA.

Why the standard error depends on by

Scores on rows from the same group, fold or forecast origin are correlated, because those rows share whatever the model got right or wrong about them. Treating them as independent understates the standard error, and makes a difference look more certain than it is. So the standard error is computed at the level the data are dependent at:

  • by = "row": rows are independent. Right for rows with no shared structure.

  • by = a column such as "group" or "fold": a cluster-robust standard error, with the rows of a cluster summed first. This is the same as sandwich::vcovCL() with its default HC1 adjustment, applied to the differences. The test uses a t distribution with one fewer degrees of freedom than there are clusters.

  • by = "origin": rolling-origin forecasts. The differences are averaged within each origin, and those origin means are tested with a Diebold-Mariano test: pooled over the horizons, and at each horizon on its own when there are several. Forecasts from neighbouring origins overlap when the horizon is longer than one, so the origin means are autocorrelated, and the test's variance allows for it.

    • method = "wpe" (the default): the fixed-smoothing test of Coroneo and Iacone (2020). The variance is the periodogram averaged over the first m Fourier frequencies of the T origin means (their weighted periodogram estimate with the Daniell kernel, section 4.2, equation (8)), and the statistic is referred to t on 2m degrees of freedom (equation (9)). m = floor(T^(1/3)) is the bandwidth they use in their simulations (section 5). In limn's simulation (studies/findings/compare_dm_fixed.md) it held its size from 10 origins up, where the usual test rejected up to 12% of the time at 5%.

    • method = "dm": the usual test, a long-run variance truncated at lag with equal weights, the uniform lag window Diebold and Mariano (1995, section 1.1) recommend, with Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold's (1997) small-sample correction (equation (9), p. 283), referred to t on T - 1 degrees of freedom (pp. 283-284). When no fallback is needed it agrees with forecast::dm.test(), as limn's study studies/scripts/compare_dm.R checks; that package is an outside comparator, not a source. By default lag is the longest horizon minus one, the overlap when the origin moves one time point at a time. Diebold and Mariano take k - 1 as a benchmark for k-step-ahead forecasts, because optimal forecasts' errors are at most (k - 1)-dependent (section 1.1); they note that this can fail in practice. With fewer than about 100 origins over several horizons it rejects too often, and warns.

Checks

What each check means and what to do about it, in the words it is printed with. A reference supports what was found and why; a remedy draws on it only where it says so, and anything marked as limn's own reasoning is not the source's:

  • few origins (warn): The comparison has T origins over several horizons, fewer than about 100. With so few origins the usual Diebold-Mariano test rejects too often when forecasts overlap: in limn's simulation, up to 12% of the time at 5% with 50 origins or fewer (studies/findings/compare_dm_fixed.md). Reference: Coroneo and Iacone (2020), Journal of Applied Econometrics 35(4), 391-409, section 4.2 (the test) and section 5 (its bandwidth). Use method = "wpe", the reference's fixed-smoothing test, which held its size from 10 origins up in the same simulation; or compare over more origins.

  • Diebold-Mariano variance (warn): The long-run variance truncated at lag L was negative, so it was taken as 0 and the null hypothesis of equal accuracy was rejected. A long-run variance truncated with equal weights can come out negative. Diebold and Mariano's rule for that case is to take it as 0 and reject the null, so the statistic is infinite and the p-value 0. They call a negative estimate a rare event. In limn's own check against the simulation design of Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold (1997, p. 284), it arose in 35% of samples with 8 origins at horizon 5 (lag 4), and in 17% with 16, and the rule took the modified test's size at nominal 10% to 41.9% there, and to 29.7% with 8 origins at horizon 3 (lag 2), against their Table 1's 12.9% and 18.1% (p. 285) (studies/findings/compare_dm_negative.md). Reference: Diebold and Mariano (1995), Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 13, 253-263, section 1.1. Read this rejection with care, or use method = "wpe", the default, which needs no lag and held its size from 10 origins up in limn's simulation.

Catching the checks

Each check above is raised as a warning of class lmn_<id>, beside lmn_diagnostic, and is kept on the result as a row of attr(x, "checks"), a data frame whose id column names it:

  • dm_few_origins (warning class lmn_dm_few_origins): few origins over several horizons for the usual test;

  • dm_negative_variance (warning class lmn_dm_negative_variance): the truncated long-run variance was negative, so it was taken as 0 and the null hypothesis rejected.

So withCallingHandlers(ilm_compare(...), lmn_dm_negative_variance = function(w) ...) handles that warning alone, and attr(cmp, "checks")$id says which checks a comparison raised.

References

Diebold, F. X. and Mariano, R. S. (1995). Comparing predictive accuracy. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 13, 253-263. Section 1.1: the statistic, the truncated long-run variance with the uniform (rectangular) lag window they recommend, the lag k - 1 as a benchmark for k-step-ahead forecasts, and the rule for a negative estimate.

Coroneo, L. and Iacone, F. (2020). Comparing predictive accuracy in small samples using fixed-smoothing asymptotics. Journal of Applied Econometrics 35(4), 391-409. Section 4.2, equations (8) and (9): the weighted periodogram estimate and its t limit on 2m degrees of freedom; section 5: the bandwidth m = floor(T^(1/3)).

Harvey, D., Leybourne, S. and Newbold, P. (1997). Testing the equality of prediction mean squared errors. International Journal of Forecasting 13, 281-291. Equation (9), p. 283: the corrected statistic; pp. 283-284: Student's t on n - 1 degrees of freedom.

See also

ilm_folds() for folds that make scores comparable.

Examples

set.seed(1)
g <- rep(1:10, each = 5)
a <- data.frame(group = g, log = rnorm(50, 1.2) + rnorm(10)[g])
b <- data.frame(group = g, log = a$log - 0.1 + rnorm(50, 0, 0.2))
ilm_compare(reference = a, candidate = b, by = "group")
#> candidate's log score is lower than reference's by 0.0684 a row (SE 0.0354, clustered by group, 10 clusters; p = 0.0854).
#> Scores are losses: lower is better.
